# Abstract

Operation Viscount Project CENTAUR-II reconstructs the long-run demographic series of the Central Plains (USGS Hydrological Unit 11, Arkansas-White-Red drainage, `645.292 km²` across `9.311` five-arcminute cells) from `10000BC` to `1600AD`.

Combining `68` catalogued archaeological settlements with continuous rural priors interpolated from `sites_northern_america` (`93.358` unique site-periods across `4.457` domestic catchments and `171` cross-frontier buffers, a `14,12x` baseline over global radiocarbon records alone), total population rises from `1.000` in `10000BC` to `86,3k` at `0AD` and peaks at `160,0k` (`147,2k-172,8k`; `0,248` persons/km²) in `1500AD`.

Guided by Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] HU 11 summed radiocarbon curve (`N = 1.549` terrestrial dates, median peak `1483AD`, `467 cal BP`), sub-regional maxima diverge sharply in timing. The Lower Arkansas and Red River Caddoan zone peaked at `1300AD` (`58,5k`) around Spiro and related mound centres before easing to `52,0k` in `1500AD`, whereas the Middle Arkansas Wichita prairies (`72,0k`) and High Plains (`36,0k`) continued growing through `1500AD`.

Following mid-sixteenth-century Spanish expeditions and Old World epidemic spread along Southern Plains exchange routes, regional population declined by `21,88%` from `1500AD` to `125,0k` (`115,0k-135,0k`; `0,194` persons/km²) in `1600AD` [@vehik2002wichita; @perttula1992caddo; @jones2014].

# Background

## Prairie Gradient and Earlier Continental Limitations

Earlier continental population atlases smoothed indigenous North American density across broad longitudinal zones or fixed post-contact multiplication ratios, flattening the pronounced moisture and agrarian gradient spanning USGS Hydrological Unit 11 [@ubelaker2006; @milner2010]. Across these `645,29k km²` of the Arkansas, Canadian, Cimarron, White and upper Red river drainages, mean precipitation triples from semi-arid Llano Estacado shortgrass steppe in the west to humid Ozark and Ouachita oak-hickory lowlands in the east.

Archaeological records across this transect establish three distinct demographic regimes rather than a uniform bison-nomad hinterland. Along the Lower Arkansas, White and Red River Great Bend, Woodland mound builders at `Toltec Mounds` gave way after `950AD` to ranked Caddoan and Mississippian chiefdoms anchored at `Spiro`, `Harlan`, `Crenshaw`, `Battle Mound` and `Carden Bottoms` [@rolingson1998toltec; @brown1996spiro; @perttula1992caddo].

Across central Oklahoma and Kansas, Plains Village horticulturalists along the Washita, Canadian and middle Arkansas valleys constructed semi-sedentary grass-and-thatch hamlets that coalesced during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries into populous Wichita towns such as `Etzanoa` and `Tobias-Quivira` [@drass1997washita; @wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita]. On the western High Plains caprock, `Antelope Creek-Alibates` flint quarries and stone-slab farmsteads pulsed with Southern Plains maize cultivation between `1200AD` and `1500AD` before drought contraction returned much of the shortgrass steppe to specialised bison hunting [@lintz1986antelope].

## Radiocarbon Timing Across HU 11

Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] demonstrated that HU 11 did not experience a uniform demographic collapse contemporaneous with the American Bottom around `1150-1250AD`. Instead, `N = 1.549` screened terrestrial radiocarbon dates across the Arkansas-White-Red drainage generate a summed probability peak at `467 cal BP` (`1483AD`, interquartile range `436` to `484 cal BP`).

This late fifteenth-century basin-wide crest reconciles apparent contradictions in the regional archaeological record. Although monumental burial ceremonialism at `Spiro` peaked around `1300-1350AD` and Lower Arkansas mound building ebbed during the fifteenth century [@brown1996spiro], demographic weight shifted northward and westward into coalescent Wichita farming aggregations across the Arkansas-Walnut and Little Arkansas confluences [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita].

## Climate Shocks, Geoarchaeology and Palaeoecological Benchmarks

Separating climatic contraction from archaeological visibility loss requires benchmark comparisons across Holocene dryland and temperate interiors. Multi-proxy reconstructions of drought-driven urban contraction [@lawrence2021collapse] and catastrophic coastal or flood disruption [@shtienberg2020neolithic] underline how short-lived aridity pulses reorganise rather than uniformly extinguish settlement networks.

On the western plains margin, Late Pleistocene horse tooth morphology and ancient DNA establish the ecological baseline of megafaunal turnover prior to Holocene bison-hunting intensification [@barronortiz2017cheek], while prey body-size indices [@marom2013prey; @munro2022revisiting] and isotopic dietary series [@gamarra2018years; @stojanovski2020living] demonstrate how sedentary villagers balanced maize cropping with persistent large-mammal hunting. High-resolution alluvial sediment micromorphology [@nicosia2022high] and palaeoriver geoarchaeology [@groucutt2025novel] further explain why deeply buried Arkansas and Red river terraces under-represent Early and Middle Holocene occupations unless adjusted spatially.

## Ecological Zonation Between Shortgrass Steppe and Ouachita Woodlands

Hydrological Unit 11 encompasses nearly seven degrees of latitude (`31,73 N` to `38,68 N`) and more than fourteen degrees of longitude (`90,51 W` to `104,58 W`). Precipitation increases steadily from semi-arid New Mexico and Texas caprock breaks toward humid Arkansas lowlands, creating sharp gradients in frost-free growing seasons and timber cover.

That moisture gradient separated western caprock communities, where dry-farmed plots faced recurring drought risk around `1350-1450AD`, from eastern river valleys buffered by oak mast, fish-bearing oxbow lakes and alluvial bottomlands [@brown1996spiro; @lintz1986antelope]. Any uniform steppe density multiplier obscures this split.

Accounting simultaneously for valley-floor aggregation and upland hunting range requires integrating site-specific town chronologies with spatially continuous radiocarbon priors tuned to local hydrography.

# Methodology

## Sub-Regional Partition and Areal Masks

CENTAUR-II partitions HU 11 (`9.311` five-arcminute active cells, `645.292 km²`, spanning `31,73 N` to `38,68 N` and `90,51 W` to `104,58 W`) into three hydrological and ecological sub-regions (Table \ref{tab:cp-structure}):

1. **Upper Arkansas, Cimarron and Llano Estacado High Plains** (`cp_high_plains_upper_arkansas`, `288.294 km²`, `44,68%`, `4.163` cells, `18` catalogued sites): encompasses western Kansas, the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, southeastern Colorado and northeastern New Mexico, including Palaeoindian bison kills (`Miami`, `Folsom`, `Lipscomb`, `Olsen-Chubbuck`) and stone-slab farmsteads around `Antelope Creek-Alibates` [@lintz1986antelope].
2. **Middle Arkansas, Neosho-Grand, Canadian and Washita Prairies** (`cp_neosho_verdigris_washita_prairies`, `194.550 km²`, `30,15%`, `2.817` cells, `23` catalogued sites): covers central Kansas and Oklahoma tallgrass and mixed prairies, capturing Washita River hamlets and the coalescent Wichita towns `Etzanoa`, `Tobias-Quivira`, `Little River` and `Deer Creek` [@drass1997washita; @wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita].
3. **Lower Arkansas Valley, Ozark Fringe and Red River Bend** (`cp_arkansas_valley_ozark_spiro`, `162.448 km²`, `25,17%`, `2.331` cells, `27` catalogued sites): integrates eastern Oklahoma, western and central Arkansas, southwestern Missouri and adjacent Red River counties anchored by `Toltec Mounds`, `Spiro`, `Harlan`, `Crenshaw`, `Battle Mound`, `Hatchel` and `Carden Bottoms` [@rolingson1998toltec; @brown1996spiro; @perttula1992caddo].

## Multi-Registry Radiocarbon Kriging and Benchmark Calibration

Rural habitation weights across HU 11 come from `sites_northern_america`, which harmonises `p3k14c` [@bird2022p3k14c], `c14bazAAR`, state site-file registries and CRM inventories into `93.358` unique site-period observations spanning `4.457` domestic Voronoi catchments (`2.678` active inhabited catchments, median radius `27,36 km`, 90th percentile `59,92 km`) plus `171` cross-frontier buffer catchments.

This composite offers a `14,12x` spatial observation multiplier over raw continental radiocarbon entries alone. Site densities are transformed via Freeman-Tukey variance stabilisation, macro-tile log-variance regularisation and 1-ring Poisson-Gamma credibility shrinkage before weighted least-squares (WLS) covariate regression and non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging [@paciorek2006matern].

Biophysical covariates capture steep prairie aridity gradients using `13,5 km` fluvial distance decay, exponential coastal proximity, terrain slope and habitable cell fraction. Bayesian phase boundaries [@crema2021rcarbon; @ramos2023revision; @burley2018early] and craft-specialisation proxies [@thuesen2023nascent] justify treating dated habitation intensity strictly as relative rural suitability rather than raw per-capita headcounts.

## Temporal Horizon Interpolation and Frontier Smoothing

Whereas `central_plains.json5` tabulates `23` demographic benchmarks between `10000BC` and `1600AD`, `sites_northern_america` constructs non-stationary kriging surfaces across `10` canonical Holocene slices (`10000BC`, `8000BC`, `5000BC`, `3000BC`, `2000BC`, `1000BC`, `0AD`, `1000AD`, `1300AD` and `1600AD`). Intermediate Woodland and sixteenth-century intervals receive linearly blended spatial weight surfaces normalised within each sub-regional mask.

Cross-frontier `300 km` buffer catchments bridge HU 11 smoothly across artificial hydrological borders: westward into Rio Grande and Pecos tributaries, northward into Platte-Republican Central Plains sites, and eastward along the Ouachita, Red and Mississippi bottomlands toward HU 08 and HU 07.

## Urban Subtraction and Uncertainty Intervals

For each sub-region $r$ and benchmark horizon $t \in \{-10000, \dots, 1600\}$, catalogued town populations summed across all `68` sites in `central_plains_settlements.json` are subtracted from sub-regional targets $P_r(t)$ prior to rural allocation:

$$R_r(t) = P_r(t) - \sum_{i \in S_r} U_i(t), \qquad R_r(t) \ge 0$$

Rural residuals $R_r(t)$ distribute proportionally across active five-arcminute cells according to the interpolated `sites_northern_america` Matérn weights and undergo two separable `5`-pixel smoothing passes. Symmetric `±8,0%` interval bounds (`[0,92 P_r(t), 1,08 P_r(t)]`) reflect alluvial site-burial uncertainty and sixteenth-century Spanish eyewitness league variance across dispersed Wichita grass-lodge compounds [@wedel1982quivira].

# Testing and Validation

Five verification gates pass with `0` errors at `GMT+0`:

1. **Radiocarbon Sample Threshold**: HU 11 rests on `N = 1.549` terrestrial radiocarbon dates [@kelly2025], nearly four times the `400`-date reliability floor required for two-millennium peak estimation [@crema2021rcarbon].
2. **Non-Stationary Kriging Sharpness**: Across all ten horizons of `sites_northern_america`, the Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) variogram satisfies $\tau_1 = 1,41$ (`1,4144`), $\tau_2 = 2,62$ (`2,6166`), effective short range `38,7 km`, raw nugget `0,000`, regularised nugget-to-sill `0,04` (`< 0,45`) and WLS fit $R^2 = 0,999$ (`0,9991` to `0,9993`).
3. **Gazetteer and Ledger Reconciliation**: Cross-checking `central_plains_settlements.json` (`68` included settlements: `18` in High Plains, `23` in Middle Arkansas and `27` in Lower Arkansas) against `central_plains_source_ledger.json5` (`69` candidate records, `1` excluded duplicate alias of `Battle Mound`) yields `0` unmatched keys and `0` coordinate errors.
4. **Urban-Rural Mass Conservation**: Summed settlement populations stay strictly within sub-regional targets at every benchmark, growing from `95` of `4.250` inhabitants (`2,24%`) at `8000BC` and `830` (`0,69%`) at `600AD` to `9.680` (`6,12%` of `158,2k`) in `1300AD`, `15.770` (`9,86%` of `160,0k`) in `1500AD`, `23.550` (`16,53%` of `142,5k`) in `1550AD` and `27.440` (`21,95%` of `125,0k`) in `1600AD`.
5. **Arithmetic Benchmark Consistency**: Sub-regional series and `92%` confidence bounds sum identically to `headline_population_by_benchmark` across all `23` horizons (`10000BC` to `1600AD`).

# Results

## Palaeoindian Bison Kill Horizons and Archaic Prairie Expansion

Following retreat of Pleistocene ice sheets and megafaunal turnover across western valleys, early Holocene archaeology across HU 11 anchors one of the continent's oldest documented bison-procurement landscapes.

Palaeoindian camps and kill sites along the Llano Estacado and Southern High Plains margins - including `Miami` (`9500BC-9200BC`), `Cooper Bison Kill` (`9200BC-8400BC`), `Lipscomb` (`8900BC-8600BC`), `Folsom` (`8700BC-8300BC`), `Olsen-Chubbuck` (`8300BC-7100BC`) and `Winger` (`7100BC-6600BC`) - register small mobile bands (`30` to `75` people per aggregation) harvesting late glacial *Bison antiquus* herds [@barronortiz2017cheek].

Total HU 11 population grew slowly from `1.000` (`920-1.080`; `0,002` persons/km²) in `10000BC` and `4.250` (`3.910-4.590`) in `8000BC` to `19,6k` in `5000BC`, `39,4k` in `3000BC` and `52,7k` in `2000BC`.

Archaic prairie camps such as `William Young` (`4800BC-1200BC`) exploited gallery forests, spring-fed bison wallows and Alibates chert outcrops across both mixed prairies and Ozark uplands. Broad-spectrum plant processing, nut harvesting and deer hunting supported slow, continuous growth across `3000BC-1000BC` (`39,4k` up to `68,3k`) ahead of pottery introduction.

By `0AD`, regional population stood at `86,3k` (`79,4k-93,2k`; `0,134` persons/km²), with `33,0k` (`38,24%`) residing in the humid Lower Arkansas and Red River lowlands against `31,5k` (`36,50%`) on the Middle Arkansas prairies and `21,8k` (`25,26%`) across the semi-arid High Plains (Figure \ref{fig:traj-central-plains}).

## Woodland Ceremonial Centres and Caddoan Mound Climax

Across the Middle and Late Woodland (`200AD-1000AD`), regional totals rose steadily from `97,5k` in `200AD` to `120,7k` in `600AD`, `132,0k` in `800AD` and `141,4k` in `1000AD`. In the Lower Arkansas Valley, Plum Bayou earthwork planners raised sixteen-mound civic-ceremonial complexes led by `Toltec Mounds` (`1.450` at `800AD`, active `600AD-1000AD`), establishing fixed floodplain ritual capitals well ahead of Mississippian shell-tempered pottery [@rolingson1998toltec].

Between `950AD` and `1350AD`, Caddoan ceremonial polities reshaped the eastern third of HU 11. `Harlan` (`980` at `1100AD`), `Crenshaw` (`980` at `1150AD`) and `Norman` (`740` at `1150AD`) transitioned into the premier regional necropolis at `Spiro` (`3.100` at `1350AD`, active `900AD-1450AD`), paired southward along the Red River Great Bend with `Battle Mound` (`1.650` at `1400AD`), `Hatchel` (`1.100` at `1450AD`), `Roitsch` (`920` at `1400AD`) and `Belcher` (`780` at `1400AD`) [@brown1996spiro; @perttula1992caddo].

Driven by Caddoan intensification, the Lower Arkansas-Spiro sub-region attained its Holocene peak of `58,5k` (`53,8k-63,2k`; `0,360` persons/km², `36,98%` of HU 11) in `1300AD`, roughly `150-200` years before western prairie and High Plains trajectories topped out (Table \ref{tab:cp-subregions}).

## Prairie Coalescence, High Plains Expansion and Sixteenth-Century Shift

While Caddoan mound construction waned after `1400AD` (`55,0k` in `1400AD` down to `52,0k` in `1500AD`), demographic growth accelerated across the Middle Arkansas prairies and Washita-Canadian basins [@drass1997washita; @vehik2002wichita]. Middle Arkansas population rose from `55,5k` in `1000AD` to `65,5k` in `1300AD`, `69,0k` in `1400AD` and a sub-regional peak of `72,0k` (`66,2k-77,8k`; `0,370` persons/km², `45,00%` of HU 11) in `1500AD` (Figure \ref{fig:shares-central-plains}).

On the High Plains caprock, Plains Village farmsteads around `Antelope Creek-Alibates` (`1.200` at `1300AD`, anchored near quarry sources occupied intermittently since `8000BC`) and `Buried City` (`680` at `1300AD`) expanded maize-and-bison storage economies before fifteenth-century drought thinned stone-slab hamlets [@lintz1986antelope]. Broad High Plains bison-hunting bands pushed that western sub-region to a `36,0k` peak (`0,125` persons/km²) in `1500AD`, lifting HU 11 as a whole to its Holocene maximum of `160,0k` (`147,2k-172,8k`; `0,248` persons/km²) in `1500AD`, closely matching the `1483AD` Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] radiocarbon peak.

This divergence highlights the east-west hydraulic asymmetry of the basin: Caddoan ceremonial towns in humid eastern valleys consolidated and devolved early, whereas tallgrass prairie villages expanded along alluvial floodplains capable of anchoring both bison procurement and reliable garden plots.

In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, dispersed Wichita hamlets consolidated along the Arkansas-Walnut and Little Arkansas corridors for mutual defence against encroaching equestrian-era precursors and neighbouring Plains raiders [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita]. Coalescent towns ballooned even as rural peripheries thinned: `Etzanoa` (`37,06 N, 97,00 W`) reached `14,0k` by `1600AD`, joined by `Tobias-Quivira` (`3.600` at `1550AD`), `Tobias` (`1.400`), `Little River` (`1.180`), `Malone` (`1.100`), `Deer Creek` (`980`) and `Sharps Creek` (`950`) (Table \ref{tab:cp-top-sites}).

Consequently, Middle Arkansas's urbanised share surged from `2,89%` (`1.890` of `65,5k`) in `1300AD` and `16,25%` (`11.700` of `72,0k`) in `1500AD` to `43,32%` (`24.690` of `57,0k`) in `1600AD`. Following Coronado's `1541AD` entrada and Oñate's `1601AD` encounter, Old World pathogens and bison-trade warfare reduced HU 11 from `160,0k` in `1500AD` to `142,5k` in `1550AD` and `125,0k` (`0,194` persons/km²) in `1600AD` (`21,88%` decline) [@ubelaker2006; @jones2014; @milner2010].

## Settlement Primacy and Urban-Rural Balance

Across all `68` catalogued settlements in HU 11, rank-size hierarchy shifted dramatically between `1300AD` and `1600AD`. During the Caddoan climax, secondary centres (`Spiro` at `3.100`, `Battle Mound` at `1.650`, `Hatchel` at `1.100`) formed a relatively flat eastern mound tier capturing just `6,12%` (`9.680` of `158,2k`) of basin population.

By `1600AD`, coalescence into fortified Wichita macro-towns along the Arkansas-Walnut confluence lifted total urbanised population to `27.440` (`21,95%` of `125,0k`), even while the western High Plains lost every nucleated stone-slab town (`1.880` in `1300AD` down to `0` by `1550AD`).

That spatial shift demonstrates how regional population stability near the eastern prairie ecotone masked acute western contraction after `1450AD`. Between `1300AD` and `1600AD`, the centre of urban gravity shifted nearly `400 km` northwestward from the Arkansas Valley into the middle Arkansas plains.

This geographic migration reconciles earlier archaeological syntheses that treated eastern Caddoan depopulation as basin-wide abandonment [@brown1996spiro; @vehik2002wichita]. Even as monumental mound precincts closed in Arkansas and eastern Oklahoma, aggregated Wichita settlements absorbed high regional densities further upstream.

## Sub-Regional Trajectories Across the Three Tiers

### Upper Arkansas, Cimarron and Llano Estacado High Plains

Spanning `288.294 km²` (`44,68%` of HU 11), the western caprock grew from `350` inhabitants (`322-378`) in `10000BC` to `5,9k` in `5000BC` and `21,8k` (`0,076` persons/km²) by `0AD`. Mobile Archaic bison-hunting bands depended on canyon springs, playa lakes and Alibates silicified-dolomite outcrops along the Canadian River breaks [@lintz1986antelope; @barronortiz2017cheek].

Late prehistoric horticultural expansion carried the sub-region from `31,4k` in `1000AD` to `34,2k` in `1300AD` (`Antelope Creek-Alibates` `1.200`, `Buried City` `680`), peaking modestly at `36,0k` (`33,1k-38,9k`; `0,125` persons/km²) in `1500AD` as specialised bison nomads replaced abandoned stone-slab hamlets. Post-`1500AD` raiding and Old World contagion lowered western numbers to `33,0k` in `1550AD` and `30,0k` (`0,104` persons/km²) by `1600AD` [@jones2014].

### Middle Arkansas, Neosho-Grand, Canadian and Washita Prairies

Encompassing `194.550 km²` (`30,15%` of HU 11), central Oklahoma and Kansas rose from `300` inhabitants in `10000BC` and `6,5k` in `5000BC` to `31,5k` (`0,162` persons/km²) at `0AD` and `55,5k` in `1000AD`. Washita River Plains Village farmers multiplied along rich sandy river terraces during the twelfth to fourteenth centuries (`65,5k` in `1300AD`), pairing riverbottom maize with tallgrass bison hunts [@drass1997washita].

Fifteenth-century coalescence around the Great Bend of the Arkansas lifted this middle tier to a peak of `72,0k` (`66,2k-77,8k`; `0,370` persons/km², `45,00%` of all HU 11 inhabitants) in `1500AD`, nearly three times High Plains rural density [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita]. Subsequent disease outbreaks following `1541AD` dropped totals to `64,5k` (`1550AD`) and `57,0k` (`0,293` persons/km²) by `1600AD`, with `43,32%` concentrated inside `Etzanoa` (`14,0k`), `Tobias-Quivira`, `Tobias`, `Little River`, `Malone`, `Deer Creek` and `Sharps Creek`.

### Lower Arkansas Valley, Ozark Fringe and Red River Bend

Across `162.448 km²` (`25,17%` of HU 11), eastern lowland density advanced earliest, rising from `350` in `10000BC` and `7,2k` in `5000BC` to `33,0k` (`0,203` persons/km²) by `0AD` and `54,5k` in `1000AD`. Floodplain oxbows and oak-hickory mast supported `Toltec Mounds` (`1.450` at `800AD`), followed by Caddoan mound networks at `Harlan`, `Crenshaw`, `Norman`, `Spiro` (`3.100` at `1350AD`), `Battle Mound` (`1.650` at `1400AD`) and `Hatchel` (`1.100` at `1450AD`) [@rolingson1998toltec; @brown1996spiro].

After reaching its sub-regional zenith of `58,5k` (`53,8k-63,2k`; `0,360` persons/km²) at `1300AD`, the Caddoan core eased to `55,0k` (`1400AD`) and `52,0k` (`1500AD`) as late fourteenth-century droughts altered Arkansas Valley political integration [@perttula1992caddo; @lawrence2021collapse]. Downstream De Soto-route epidemics (`1541-1543AD`) then accelerated contraction to `45,0k` in `1550AD` and `38,0k` (`0,234` persons/km²) in `1600AD` [@ubelaker2006; @milner2010].

### Sixteenth-Century Chronicles and Regional Border Continuity

Between `1541AD` and `1601AD`, Coronado's and Oñate's expeditions provided first-hand league and grass-lodge enumerations across the Great Bend and Walnut River settlements while Soto's Chroniclers traversed Arkansas Valley towns such as `Carden Bottoms` (`1.450` at `1500AD`) [@wedel1982quivira; @perttula1992caddo].

Across watershed divides, `300 km` cross-frontier buffers inside `sites_northern_america` align eastern Ozark and Red River densities continuously with HU 08 (`Lower Mississippi`) and HU 07 (`Upper Mississippi`), while damping artificial drops between the Arkansas headwaters and the Rio Grande border of HU 13.

# Limitations

Across HU 11, archaeological preservation biases interact strongly with soil moisture and alluvial sedimentation regimes, making transparent error stratification indispensable for downstream historical syntheses.

Four evidentiary limitations qualify the HU 11 demographic series:

1. **Alluvial Floodplain Burial**: Deep Holocene meander belts and rapid overbank alluviation along the lower Arkansas, Canadian and Red rivers conceal Archaic and Early Woodland sites beneath thick alluvium, depressing recovery relative to deflated High Plains blowouts [@rolingson1998toltec; @nicosia2022high].

2. **Mobile Bison-Hunter Radiocarbon Scarcity**: Following `1450AD` drought abandonment of semi-sedentary Plains Village hamlets on the western steppe, mobile bison-hunting camps generated far fewer charcoal features per capita than sedentary earthlodge or stone-slab houses [@lintz1986antelope; @drass1997washita].

3. **Spanish Entrada Headcount Variance**: Protohistoric Wichita town figures (`Etzanoa`, `Tobias-Quivira`) rely heavily on `1541AD` and `1601AD` Spanish chronicles whose league counts and grass-lodge tallies span wide compound areas [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita].

4. **Cross-Border Caddoan Continuity**: Southeastern Caddoan lineages along the Red River Great Bend interacted continuously with Lower Mississippi Valley centres beyond HU 11; sub-regional estimates across the eastern Ozark-Red River boundary therefore depend on the `300 km` `sites_northern_america` smoothing buffers to avoid edge discontinuities [@perttula1992caddo].

# Conclusion

The Central Plains (HU 11) exemplifies asynchronous indigenous demographic development within a single continental watershed. Early Caddoan agricultural intensification propelled Lower Arkansas-Spiro densities to a `1300AD` summit (`58,5k`), nearly two centuries before the central prairies (`72,0k`) and High Plains (`36,0k`) lifted the watershed as a whole to its `160,0k` (`0,248` persons/km²) zenith around `1500AD`.

Fifteenth- and sixteenth-century prairie coalescence concentrates nearly half of all Middle Arkansas inhabitants into fortified Wichita river towns (`24.690` of `57,0k` in `1600AD`), even as early colonial contact and epidemics initiated a `21,88%` regional downturn after `1500AD`.

Western shortgrass plains abandoned permanent masonry architecture by `1500AD`, shifting toward specialised bison-hunting economies well ahead of widespread equestrian adoption. That dual transformation explains how basin-wide demographic numbers plateaued between `1300AD` and `1500AD` despite acute sub-regional upheaval.

Pairing `68` settlements (Table \ref{tab:cp-top-sites}) with `sites_northern_america` (`93.358` site-periods) captures this west-to-east ecological split while conserving basin-wide mass across every benchmark from `10000BC` to `1600AD` [@kelly2025; @ubelaker2006]. Future stratified alluvial cores from the Washita, Canadian and Arkansas terraces can enter the spatial prior directly without revising aggregate town totals.

More broadly, the Central Plains sequence demonstrates how indigenous North American demography sustained regional peaks after `1400AD` even as major Mississippian mound centres contracted eastward. Combining radiocarbon probability envelopes with site-level town series captures both long-term rural carrying capacity and late pre-contact urban coalescence across the Arkansas-Red drainage.
